question: The Vijayanagar kingdom, whose capital stood on the Tungabhadra, was founded in 1336 by:
option_1: <style> @font-face { font-family: 'Hari'; src: url('https://static-appxdb-v2.akamai.net.in/fonts/HARI.TTF') format('truetype');} </style>Harihara I and Bukka
option_4: Deva Raya I and Deva Raya II
solution_text:
The correct answer is Harihara I and Bukka.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Vijayanagar, the 'City of Victory', was established in 1336 by the brothers Harihara I and Bukka, who began the Sangama dynasty (तुंगभद्रा तट पर विजयनगर की स्थापना — हरिहर प्रथम और बुक्का)

 

• According to tradition the brothers had been taken to Delhi by Muhammad bin Tughlaq and later sent back south to put down a revolt; instead they set up their own state.

 

• They were guided by the sage Vidyaranya and returned to Hinduism, which gave the new kingdom a strong Hindu political and cultural identity.

 

• The dynasty they founded ruled until about 1485, after which the Saluva and Tuluva houses took over.

 

• The founding brothers were originally feudatories who, as the notes record, passed through Delhi service and then returned south, so the new kingdom was born out of the Tughlaq period's revolts in the Deccan.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Harihara I held the capital first at Anegondi before the city of Vijayanagar (Hampi) grew on the south bank of the river.

 

• Bukka I (c. 1356-77) extended the kingdom and clashed repeatedly with the Bahmani sultans of Gulbarga.

 

• Four dynasties - Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva and Aravidu - ruled the empire in that order.

 

• Hampi, the capital, lies in present Karnataka and is today a World Heritage Site.

 

• The Vijayanagar rulers took the title Rayas, and the kingdom stayed a bulwark of Hindu rule in the south until the sixteenth century.

 

NOTE

 

• Krishnadevaraya and Achyuta Raya (Option 2): Krishnadevaraya (1509-29) and Achyuta Raya belonged to the Tuluva line, which came to power nearly two centuries after the city had been founded, so neither could have started it.

 

• Saluva Narasimha and Tirumala (Option 3): Saluva Narasimha began the second dynasty around 1485-86, and Tirumala founded the fourth, the Aravidu house; neither belongs to the founding generation of 1336.

 

• Deva Raya I and Deva Raya II (Option 4): Deva Raya I and Deva Raya II were later Sangama kings in the fifteenth century; they governed an already established empire rather than creating it.

question: Hampi, the ruined capital of Vijayanagar, stands on the banks of which river?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Tungabhadra.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The city of Vijayanagar, today's Hampi in Karnataka, was built on the southern bank of the Tungabhadra river amid boulder-strewn hills (हम्पी तुंगभद्रा नदी के किनारे स्थित है)

 

• The river and the rocky terrain gave natural defence, while kings such as Krishnadevaraya built tanks and canals on the Tungabhadra to irrigate the surrounding land.

 

• The same river also formed one side of the Raichur Doab, the fertile tract that the Vijayanagar kings and the Bahmani sultans fought over for generations.

 

• Hampi's ruins include the Virupaksha, Vitthala and Hazara Rama temples and are a World Heritage Site.

 

• Because Hampi sat on the south bank, the river served both as a moat and as a water source for the irrigation channels that fed fields around the capital, which helped the city sustain a very large population.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Tungabhadra is formed by the Tunga and Bhadra rivers and joins the Krishna, so the two rivers bound the Raichur Doab.

 

• Hampi is also associated with the Ramayana's Kishkindha tradition and the Pampa river name.

 

• UNESCO listed the Group of Monuments at Hampi in 1986.

 

• The river rises in the Western Ghats and flows north-east to join the Krishna near Kurnool.

 

• Its southern side holds Hampi's temples, while the northern side lies close to the Anegondi area of the early capital.

 

NOTE

 

• Krishna (Option 1): The Krishna forms the northern boundary of the Raichur Doab but not the site of the capital; Hampi lies well south of it, beside the Tungabhadra, one of the Krishna's tributaries.

 

• Godavari (Option 2): The Godavari flows through Maharashtra, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh further north, far from Vijayanagar, and was never the river of the empire's capital.

 

• Kaveri (Option 3): The Kaveri waters the Tamil country and Mysore, which came under Vijayanagar governors later; Hampi itself was never located on the Kaveri.

question: Hampi, the capital of the Vijayanagara Empire, is said to have derived its name from:
option_1: <style> @font-face { font-family: 'Hari'; src: url('https://static-appxdb-v2.akamai.net.in/fonts/HARI.TTF') format('truetype');} </style>Harihara, the founder of the empire
option_3: <style> @font-face { font-family: 'Hari'; src: url('https://static-appxdb-v2.akamai.net.in/fonts/HARI.TTF') format('truetype');} </style>Bukka, the brother of Harihara
solution_text:
The correct answer is Pampadevi, the local mother goddess.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The name Hampi is a corruption of Pampa, the old name of the Tungabhadra, and of Pampadevi, the local mother goddess associated with the site (हम्पी का नाम स्थानीय देवी पम्पादेवी से पड़ा)

 

• Pampadevi was worshipped here long before the empire; local tradition links her to her marriage with Virupaksha, a form of Shiva.

 

• Virupaksha, also called Pampapati, became the patron deity of the Vijayanagar kings, who signed their grants with the name of Virupaksha.

 

• The founders Harihara and Bukka gave the city its imperial name Vijayanagara, but the settlement's popular name kept the goddess's name.

 

• This local goddess is mentioned in the tradition of the area as Pampa, whose shrine stood beside the river long before the empire's kings built the grand temples that dominate the ruins today.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Virupaksha temple at Hampi is dedicated to Shiva and is one of the few shrines in continuous worship.

 

• Inscriptions and later foreign accounts spell the capital variously as Bisnaga or Vijayanagara.

 

• Kings used the title 'Hindu Rayasuratrana', meaning protector of Hindu kings, in their records.

 

• Vijayanagara means City of Victory, and the two names Hampi and Vijayanagara are used for the same site.

 

• The capital's sacred centre lay on the south bank of the river, near the Pampa shrine and Virupaksha's temple.

 

NOTE

 

• Harihara, the founder of the empire (Option 1): Harihara founded the empire and gave the city its royal name, Vijayanagara; the shorter popular name Hampi, however, comes from the older river and goddess name, not from the king.

 

• Bukka, the brother of Harihara (Option 3): Bukka, Harihara's brother and successor, strengthened the kingdom, but no tradition derives the name Hampi from him; the word comes from Pampa, the local goddess.

 

• Virupaksha, the tutelary deity (Option 4): Virupaksha was the empire's tutelary deity and has a great temple at Hampi, yet he is a Shaiva form; the place-name itself is traced to the goddess Pampadevi, who is linked with him by marriage.

question: Which saint is traditionally credited with inspiring Harihara and Bukka to re-convert to Hinduism and found Vijayanagar?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Vidyaranya.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• According to the tradition recorded in the notes, the brothers returned to Hinduism under the influence of Vidyaranya, the sage-scholar of Sringeri (विद्यारण्य — विजयनगर के संस्थापकों के मार्गदर्शक)

 

• This re-conversion followed their earlier stay in Delhi, where Muhammad bin Tughlaq is said to have converted them to Islam.

 

• Vidyaranya's role gave the kingdom the character of a defender of Hindu dharma against the sultanates of the north and the Deccan.

 

• He is often linked with the Sringeri monastery and with Sanskrit scholarship at the Sangama court.

 

• His influence also explains why the early kings sought legitimacy as protectors of Hindu dharma; later kings continued to give grants to Sringeri and other religious establishments in the south.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Vidyaranya, also known as Madhava, is associated with the commentaries ascribed to Sayana, the Vedic scholar of Bukka's court.

 

• The Sangama dynasty was named after Sangama, the father of Harihara and Bukka.

 

• Foreign travellers such as Abdur Razzak later described Vijayanagar as a Hindu kingdom of great wealth.

 

• Sayana, the famed commentator on the Vedas, is linked with the court of Bukka I.

 

• Sringeri in Karnataka remains the seat of the Advaita monastery founded by Adi Shankaracharya.

 

NOTE

 

• Ramanuja (Option 1): Ramanuja was an eleventh-twelfth century Vaishnava philosopher of Tamil Nadu who lived roughly two centuries before Vijayanagar was founded, so he could not have guided the brothers.

 

• Basavanna (Option 2): Basavanna was the twelfth-century founder of the Lingayat movement in Karnataka under the Kalachuri king Bijjala; he too belongs to an earlier age than the 1336 foundation.

 

• Nimbarka (Option 3): Nimbarka was a Vaishnava teacher of the Dvaitadvaita school associated with Mathura and the Braj region, with no known role in the political rise of Vijayanagar in the south.

question: Who is regarded as the greatest ruler of the Sangama dynasty of Vijayanagar?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Deva Raya II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Deva Raya II is regarded as the greatest Sangama king; after his death the dynasty grew weak and was overthrown (संगम वंश का सर्वश्रेष्ठ शासक — देवराय द्वितीय)

 

• His reign saw the visit of the Persian envoy Abdur Razzak, whose account describes Vijayanagar as a city of vast wealth and impressive fortifications.

 

• He strengthened the army by recruiting Muslim archers and cavalry and extended Vijayanagar influence over parts of South India.

 

• The Sangama line lasted from 1336 to about 1485, after which the Saluvas seized power.

 

• Under him the Vijayanagar army gained strength through the recruitment of Muslim cavalry and archers, and his rule saw the kingdom hold off the Bahmani sultans while extending its influence into coastal Andhra and Kerala.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Deva Raya II also bore the title Praudha Deva Raya and the epithet Gajabetekara, 'the elephant hunter'.

 

• Harihara I and Bukka I were the founders; Bukka I clashed with Mohammad Shah I of the Bahmanis.

 

• Nicolo Conti had visited earlier, in the reign of Deva Raya I.

 

• Abdur Razzak reached the capital in about 1443 as an envoy of Shah Rukh.

 

• Deva Raya II himself composed or patronised Sanskrit literature, and the court sheltered poets and scholars of Kannada, Telugu and Sanskrit.

 

NOTE

 

• Harihara I (Option 1): Harihara I was the co-founder who established the kingdom in 1336; he laid its foundations but did not take it to the height of power it reached under Deva Raya II.

 

• Bukka I (Option 3): Bukka I, brother of the founder, expanded the kingdom and fought the Bahmanis, yet tradition places the peak of Sangama strength in the early fifteenth century, not in his reign.

 

• Virupaksha II (Option 4): Virupaksha II was one of the weak last Sangama rulers whose misrule paved the way for Saluva Narasimha's usurpation, so he cannot be the dynasty's greatest king.

question: Krishnadevaraya's Telugu work Amuktamalyada describes the legendary wedding of which deity?
option_1: Lord Ranganayaka, an avatar of Vishnu
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lord Ranganayaka, an avatar of Vishnu.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Amuktamalyada, composed in Telugu by Krishnadevaraya, narrates the story of the Vaishnava saint Andal and her wedding to Lord Ranganayaka, a form of Vishnu (आमुक्तमाल्यद — कृष्णदेव राय की तेलुगु रचना)

 

• The work shows the king's scholarship and his standing as a celebrated patron of art and literature at Vijayanagar.

 

• Its title means 'one who wears and gives away the garland', pointing to Andal who offered garlands to the deity.

 

• Krishnadevaraya's court was famed for a circle of Telugu poets known as the Ashtadiggajas.

 

• The poem is a Telugu prabandha, a long narrative composition, and it illustrates the king's own mastery of the language, so that tradition calls him a poet-emperor besides being the empire's greatest conqueror.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Krishnadevaraya reigned from 1509 to 1529 and was a contemporary of Babur.

 

• He also composed Sanskrit works and is remembered by the title Andhra Bhoja.

 

• Amuktamalyada is also called Vishnuchittiya and is a prabandha in Telugu.

 

• Andal was one of the twelve Alvars, the Tamil Vaishnava saints, and her poems are the Tiruppavai.

 

• Srirangam, near Tiruchirappalli, houses the famous Ranganathaswamy temple.

 

NOTE

 

• Lord Shiva and Parvati (Option 2): The wedding of Shiva and Parvati is the subject of the Kumarasambhava of Kalidasa, a Sanskrit classical poem, not of the Telugu text composed by Krishnadevaraya.

 

• Lord Rama and Sita (Option 3): The marriage of Rama and Sita belongs to the Ramayana tradition; Amuktamalyada instead recounts a Vaishnava devotee's marriage to Ranganayaka, a form of Vishnu enshrined at Srirangam.

 

• Lord Venkateswara and Padmavati (Option 4): The union of Venkateswara and Padmavati is a Tirupati legend and was not the theme of this poem, which focuses on the saint Andal and the deity of Srirangam.

question: Allasani Peddana, called Andhra Kavita Pitamaha, was a prominent poet at the court of:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Krishnadevaraya.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Allasani Peddana was the foremost of the Ashtadiggajas, the eight poets who adorned the court of Krishnadevaraya (अल्लासानी पेड्डना — कृष्णदेव राय के दरबारी कवि)

 

• He composed the Telugu prabandha Manucharitam, a landmark of the golden age of Telugu literature under the Tuluva king.

 

• The king's own Amuktamalyada and his generous patronage of poets earned him a reputation as a great patron of art and literature.

 

• The era of Krishnadevaraya (1509-1529) is therefore remembered as the high point of literature in Vijayanagar.

 

• His Manucharitam is a prabandha on the story of Manu, and it set the model for the new style of Telugu verse that spread through the court under the Tuluva patron.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other Ashtadiggajas included Nandi Timmana, Dhurjati and Tenali Ramakrishna, with the last known for wit.

 

• Peddana's Manucharitam is also known as Swarochisha Sambhava.

 

• Telugu, Kannada, Sanskrit and Tamil literature all flourished in Vijayanagar.

 

• The Ashtadiggajas are listed in different ways, and Allasani Peddana is the one named in every list.

 

• Krishnadevaraya's court is often compared to that of Bhoja of Dhara, hence the title Andhra Bhoja.

 

NOTE

 

• Deva Raya II (Option 1): Deva Raya II was a Sangama ruler known for military strength and for hosting Abdur Razzak; the Ashtadiggajas belong to the later Tuluva court, not to his time.

 

• Rama Raya (Option 3): Rama Raya acted as the powerful regent of the Aravidu period and died at Talikota in 1565; Peddana's career was associated with the earlier reign of Krishnadevaraya.

 

• Harihara I (Option 4): Harihara I was the first king, ruling in the fourteenth century, long before Telugu prabandha poetry flourished at court; Peddana served nearly two centuries later.

question: Krishnadevaraya signed a treaty with the Portuguese governor:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Alfonso de Albuquerque.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Krishnadevaraya concluded an agreement with the Portuguese governor Alfonso de Albuquerque, who had taken Goa in 1510 (अल्फांसो डी अल्बुकर्क — पुर्तगाली गवर्नर)

 

• The alliance suited both sides: the Portuguese wanted a friendly power on the coast, while Vijayanagar wanted a steady supply of imported war horses.

 

• It shows that the empire engaged in overseas trade and diplomacy instead of avoiding the sea.

 

• The king was at the same time a great conqueror who fought the Bahmani successor states and the Gajapatis.

 

• Portuguese seapower along the Konkan and Malabar coast made the friendship valuable, as Vijayanagar could not rely on Bahmani successor states for the imported Arabian horses that its cavalry needed.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Domingo Paes, a Portuguese traveller, visited his court and described the capital in detail.

 

• Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498, earlier than Albuquerque's governorship.

 

• Albuquerque was governor of Portuguese India from 1509 to 1515.

 

• Goa was captured in 1510 from the Adil Shah of Bijapur, and it became the Portuguese capital in India.

 

• Travellers like Paes and Barbosa left detailed accounts of Vijayanagar during these years.

 

NOTE

 

• Vasco da Gama (Option 2): Vasco da Gama discovered the sea route to Calicut in 1498 as an explorer; he was not the governor who negotiated with Krishnadevaraya a decade later.

 

• Francisco de Almeida (Option 3): Francisco de Almeida was the first Portuguese viceroy in India (1505-09) and had been replaced by Albuquerque before Krishnadevaraya's treaty-making of the 1510s.

 

• Nuno da Cunha (Option 4): Nuno da Cunha became governor only in 1529 and served through the 1530s, so his term began at about the time Krishnadevaraya died and cannot account for the treaty.

question: Krishnadevaraya founded the city of Nagalapuram in memory of his:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Mother Nagaladevi.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• He founded the new city of Nagalapuram in memory of his mother Nagaladevi (नागलापुरम — माता नागलादेवी की स्मृति में बसाया गया नगर)

 

• The foundation reflects his role as a builder-king who also raised temples and gateways at Hampi and in other towns.

 

• Krishnadevaraya is credited with tanks and canals on the Tungabhadra and with the Vitthala and Hazara Rama temples.

 

• The name of the city is itself formed from the queen-mother's name, which makes it easy to recall.

 

• Naming a town after the queen-mother was a normal way for medieval kings to honour a relative, and it shows the ruler as a founder of new settlements and not only a conqueror.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Kamalapuram tank near Hampi is also attributed to him.

 

• His reign ran from 1509 to 1529 and he was a Tuluva king.

 

• Vyasatirtha was a Madhva saint honoured by the king.

 

• The area around Nagalapuram, also written Nagalapura, lay near the capital region in the Vijayanagar heartland.

 

• Krishnadevaraya's queens, Tirumaladevi and Chinnadevi, are often remembered in his inscriptions.

 

NOTE

 

• Wife Tirumaladevi (Option 1): Tirumaladevi was one of his queens, but the notes tie the new town to a parental memorial; queens like her are remembered through grants rather than through Nagalapuram.

 

• Daughter Mohanangi (Option 2): Mohanangi is commonly named as a daughter in later literary accounts, yet she is not the person whose memory Nagalapuram commemorates, and the city carries a different woman's name.

 

• Teacher Vyasatirtha (Option 4): Vyasatirtha was a spiritual guru of the Madhva order honoured at court; the town's name does not derive from a teacher but from the king's mother.

question: The famous Veerabhadra temple at Lepakshi, with its 'Hanging Pillar', is located in:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Andhra Pradesh.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Veerabhadra (Lepakshi) temple, famous for its Hanging Pillar, stands in Andhra Pradesh and is a fine example of Vijayanagar art of the Tuluva period (आंध्र प्रदेश का लेपाक्षी मंदिर — हैंगिंग पिलर)

 

• The pillar appears to hang from the ceiling with a gap beneath it, which is the main attraction for visitors.

 

• The temple is rich in murals and sculpture and shows the late Vijayanagar style of temple building.

 

• Nandi, the huge monolithic bull near the temple, is also well known.

 

• The temple was built in the Tuluva period and its mandapas, carved pillars and wall paintings reflect the local style, which is the reason the notes place it among the art and culture of the Tuluvas.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Lepakshi lies in the Anantapur (Sri Sathya Sai) district near the Karnataka border.

 

• The Virupaksha temple at Hampi, in Karnataka, is dedicated to Shiva.

 

• The Vitthala and Hazara Rama temples at Hampi carry scenes of the Ramayana and Mahabharata.

 

• The Lepakshi Nandi is among the largest monolithic bulls in India.

 

• The temple is dedicated to Veerabhadra, a ferocious form of Shiva.

 

NOTE

 

• Karnataka (Option 1): Karnataka holds Hampi and its famous temples, but the Lepakshi temple with the Hanging Pillar lies just across the border in Andhra Pradesh and should not be confused with them.

 

• Tamil Nadu (Option 2): Tamil Nadu contains Vijayanagar-era gopurams and mandapas, such as those at Vellore and Kanchipuram, yet Lepakshi itself is not located in that state.

 

• Kerala (Option 3): Kerala was never part of the Vijayanagar heartland and has no Lepakshi temple; its temple tradition developed in a very different architectural style.

question: The architect of the Gol Gumbaz, the great domed tomb at Bijapur, was:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Yakut of Dabul.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Gol Gumbaz, in Bijapur (Karnataka), was designed by Yakut of Dabul and built under the Adil Shahi dynasty in the Deccan style (गोल गुम्बद के वास्तुकार — दाभोल के याकूत)

 

• It is among the largest domed structures in India and is the tomb of Mohammad Adil Shah.

 

• Bijapur was the capital of the Adil Shahi sultans, one of the five states that emerged from the Bahmani kingdom.

 

• The huge hemispherical dome rises over a square hall, with octagonal towers at the corners.

 

• The dome is a huge hemisphere without internal supports and the monument displays the Deccan style of architecture, which draws on Persian forms as well as on local Karnataka building methods.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Its whispering gallery is a famous feature.

 

• Adil Shahi architecture is distinct from Vijayanagar temple architecture, though both share the Deccan region.

 

• The Ibrahim Rauza is another Bijapur monument.

 

• Dabul, now Dabhol, was a port on the Konkan coast.

 

• Bijapur, now called Vijayapura, was the Adil Shahi capital until Aurangzeb took it in 1686.

 

NOTE

 

• Ustad Ahmad Lahori (Option 1): Ustad Ahmad Lahori is credited with the Taj Mahal and the Red Fort under Shah Jahan, a northern Mughal context that has no link with the Bijapur tomb.

 

• Mir Mirak Mirza Ghiyas (Option 2): Mir Mirak Mirza Ghiyas designed the Humayun's Tomb in Delhi for the Mughals; his work belongs to the Persian-influenced capital style, unlike the Deccan tomb built in Bijapur.

 

• Ustad Isa (Option 4): Ustad Isa is traditionally linked with the Persian-influenced Mughal tomb tradition of Agra and is not remembered as the builder of Bijapur's great dome, which tradition gives to an architect from Dabul.

question: Who was the founder of the Saluva dynasty of Vijayanagar?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Saluva Narasimha.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The second dynasty, the Saluva line, was founded by Saluva Narasimha (Narasimha Deva Raya) around 1485-86 (सालुव वंश के संस्थापक — सालुव नरसिंह)

 

• He seized power when the late Sangama rulers had become weak after the death of Deva Raya II.

 

• The Saluva dynasty reigned only for a brief period, roughly 1486 to 1509, before it was replaced by the Tuluvas.

 

• It is therefore counted as the second of the four ruling houses of Vijayanagar.

 

• Saluva Narasimha's rise was a military takeover and the notes treat the whole Saluva period as short, so it was soon followed by the Tuluva line under Veera Narasimha.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498, during Saluva rule.

 

• The Saluva interlude lasted about two decades.

 

• The Tuluva king Krishnadevaraya came to the throne in 1509.

 

• Saluva Narasimha is known by the title Narasimha Deva Raya.

 

• The Saluva line had only two rulers of note before the Tuluvas took charge.

 

NOTE

 

• Veera Narasimha (Option 2): Veera Narasimha belonged to the Tuluva family and is credited in the notes with founding the third dynasty, not the second; the name is similar but the family differs.

 

• Tirumala (Option 3): Tirumala founded the fourth and last dynasty, the Aravidu house, in the later sixteenth century, long after the Saluvas had passed from the scene.

 

• Rama Raya (Option 4): Rama Raya was the Aravidu regent who led the army to its defeat at Talikota in 1565 and was in no way connected with the Saluva takeover.

question: The Aravidu dynasty, the fourth and last ruling house of Vijayanagar, was founded by:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Tirumala Deva Raya.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Aravidu dynasty was founded by Tirumala Deva Raya, who revived the kingdom after Talikota and shifted the seat to Penukonda (अरविदु वंश के संस्थापक — तिरुमल देवराय)

 

• His family had provided the powerful regent Rama Raya, who ruled in the name of the Tuluva puppet Sadasiva Raya.

 

• After the disaster of 1565 the kingdom survived for about another century under this house.

 

• The last ruler of the Vijayanagar kingdom was Sriranga III.

 

• Tirumala's accession shows that the empire revived after the defeat, though its capital moved away from Hampi, which had been devastated, and its political reach shrank considerably.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Aravidu rulers later moved to Chandragiri.

 

• Venkata II was among the last notable Aravidu kings.

 

• The line is counted as lasting until about 1672.

 

• Sriranga III was the last ruler of Vijayanagar in the notes' account.

 

• The empire's formal rule is counted until about 1672.

 

• Penukonda and later Chandragiri served as seats of the Aravidu kings after Hampi was ruined.

 

NOTE

 

• Sadasiva Raya (Option 1): Sadasiva Raya was the nominal Tuluva ruler kept as a figurehead while Rama Raya held actual power; he belonged to the previous line and did not start a new dynasty.

 

• Achyuta Raya (Option 2): Achyuta Raya, a brother of Krishnadevaraya, ruled in the 1530s as a Tuluva king, so he belongs to the third dynasty and had died before the Aravidu era.

 

• Sriranga III (Option 4): Sriranga III is named in the notes as the last ruler of the kingdom, not its founder; the sixteenth-century revival under Aravidu had come well before his time.

question: Palegars in the Vijayanagar empire were:
option_1: Military-cum-administrative chiefs in charge of palayams
solution_text:
The correct answer is Military-cum-administrative chiefs in charge of palayams.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Palegars were appointed by the kings as military-cum-administrative chiefs of territories called palayams; they collected revenue and kept troops (पालेगार — पालयम के सैन्य-प्रशासनिक प्रमुख)

 

• The system relied on local chiefs who served the king and supported the royal army, a feature of the Nayaka arrangement of the empire.

 

• After the decline of Vijayanagar the palegars became semi-independent.

 

• They then resisted the expansion of Mysore under Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan, and later the British.

 

• The system allowed the king to hold distant provinces with little direct administration, since each palegar was bound to pay revenue and furnish troops, and in return the chief kept a share of the revenue.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Amaram lands given to Nayakas were military fiefs.

 

• Nayaka governors later set up independent kingdoms at Madurai, Thanjavur and Gingee.

 

• Neither the iqta nor the mansabdari system operated in Vijayanagar.

 

• Veerapandiya Kattabomman of Panchalankurichi was a famous palegar who resisted the British.

 

• Poligar is the common English spelling for palegar.

 

NOTE

 

• Foreign envoys posted at Hampi (Option 2): Foreign envoys such as Abdur Razzak came as ambassadors and travellers, and they held no administrative or revenue-collecting authority; palegars were home-grown local chiefs.

 

• Temple priests of royal shrines (Option 3): Temple priests managed religious worship and endowments but not the revenue and troops of a territorial palayam, which were the chief responsibilities of the palegars.

 

• Merchants of the horse trade (Option 4): Horse traders were merchants who imported animals through the western ports; they were not appointed as territorial chiefs and did not collect land revenue.

question: The Bahmani kingdom was founded in 1347 by:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Bahmani kingdom was established in 1347 in the Deccan by Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah (also called Hasan Gangu), who broke away from Muhammad bin Tughlaq's Delhi (बहमनी राज्य की स्थापना — अलाउद्दीन बहमन शाह)

 

• He made Gulbarga the first capital; the kingdom lasted until about 1527.

 

• The state grew out of the revolt of Deccan nobles against the Delhi Sultanate and was independent from the start.

 

• Its rise gave Vijayanagar, founded eleven years earlier, a powerful northern neighbour.

 

• The founder's title Bahman Shah is believed to link him to the legendary Persian king Bahman, and the dynasty took its name from this title, which is why historians call it Bahmani.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The dynasty took its name from Bahman Shah.

 

• Gulbarga was also called Ahsanabad.

 

• The Bahmani sultans and Vijayanagar kings fought repeatedly over the Raichur Doab.

 

• Hasan Gangu rose as an officer of Muhammad bin Tughlaq in the Deccan.

 

• The Bahmani kingdom lasted from 1347 to 1527, a period of about 180 years.

 

NOTE

 

• Firoz Shah Bahmani (Option 1): Firoz Shah Bahmani was a later ruler who fought Deva Raya I and married the Vijayanagar king's daughter; he ruled long after the dynasty's founder.

 

• Ahmad Shah Wali (Option 2): Ahmad Shah Wali was another later sultan, best remembered for transferring the capital from Gulbarga to Bidar, and thus came well after the first ruler.

 

• Muhammad Shah I (Option 4): Muhammad Shah I was the son and successor of the founder; he fought Bukka I of Vijayanagar but did not establish the kingdom himself.

question: Which Bahmani ruler, known as 'Wali' (saint), shifted the capital from Gulbarga to Bidar?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ahmad Shah.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ahmad Shah, called Ahmed Shah Wali because he was regarded as a saint, moved the capital from Gulbarga to Bidar (अहमद शाह वली — राजधानी गुलबर्गा से बीदर)

 

• The notes describe him as an orthodox king, which differs from the cultured and multilingual Firoz Shah before him.

 

• Bidar, higher and more central, later became a major fortress and cultural centre, with the madrasa of Mahmud Gawan.

 

• The shift marks a second phase in Bahmani history.

 

• Ahmad Shah's religious temperament contrasts with that of Firoz Shah, who loved learning and languages, and the move to Bidar placed the capital in a cooler, more defensible position on the plateau.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ahmad Shah ruled roughly 1422-36, with Bidar becoming the capital around 1429.

 

• Bidar later gave its name to a successor state under the Barid Shahis.

 

• Gulbarga was the capital of the first Bahmani rulers.

 

• Bidar fort contains the famous Rangin Mahal and the Solah Khamba mosque.

 

• The shift is dated about 1429 in most textbooks.

 

NOTE

 

• Firoz Shah (Option 1): Firoz Shah Bahmani was multilingual, fought Deva Raya I and set up an observatory at Daulatabad; he remained at Gulbarga and did not make the move to Bidar.

 

• Muhammad Shah I (Option 2): Muhammad Shah I, the second sultan, fought Vijayanagar's Bukka I and organised the early administration at Gulbarga; the shift of capital came decades after his reign.

 

• Alauddin Bahman Shah (Option 3): Alauddin Bahman Shah founded the kingdom in 1347 with Gulbarga as capital, so he established the first seat rather than transferring it.

question: Under which Bahmani minister's reforms was the kingdom divided into eight provinces, each called a Taraf and ruled by a Tarafdar?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Mahmud Gawan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The administrative reorganisation into eight provinces (Tarafs) headed by Tarafdars is associated with Mahmud Gawan, the minister of Muhammad Shah III (तराफ़ और तराफ़दार — महमूद गवां के सुधार)

 

• Dividing the state into smaller units limited the power of provincial governors, who had grown too strong in the old large provinces.

 

• Gawan also reorganised the army and finances and founded a famous madrasa at Bidar.

 

• His reforms made the Bahmani state strong again but also angered the nobles.

 

• The notes place this reform under Mahmud Gawan and treat it as his main administrative reform, designed to curb the independence of the provincial governors.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mahmud Gawan was a Persian from Gilan and took the title Khwaja-i-Jahan.

 

• He was executed in 1481 on charges of treason.

 

• His fall deepened the quarrels between the Deccani and foreign nobles.

 

• Tarafdar was the governor of a taraf.

 

• Mahmud Gawan's madrasa at Bidar was a large centre of learning with a famous library.

 

NOTE

 

• Malik Ahmad Nizam (Option 1): Malik Ahmad Nizam was a Bahmani governor who later founded the Nizam Shahi dynasty of Ahmadnagar, not a reformer of the central provincial system.

 

• Yusuf Adil Khan (Option 2): Yusuf Adil Khan was a Bahmani officer who later became the first Adil Shahi sultan of Bijapur, so he was a founder of a successor state, not the author of Bahmani reforms.

 

• Fathullah Imad-ul-Mulk (Option 4): Fathullah Imad-ul-Mulk was the first ruler of the Imad Shahi dynasty of Berar; he declared independence after the breakdown and had no part in organising the Tarafs.

question: Mahmud Gawan, the great minister of the Bahmani kingdom, was executed in 1481 on the orders of:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Muhammad Shah III.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mahmud Gawan was put to death in 1481 by the Bahmani sultan Muhammad Shah III, whom he had long served as prime minister, after false charges of treason (महमूद गवां की हत्या — मुहम्मद शाह तृतीय के आदेश पर)

 

• The execution removed the ablest administrator of the kingdom and weakened the Sultanate.

 

• It also deepened the rift between Deccani and foreign (Afaqi) nobles, which hastened decline.

 

• By 1526 the Bahmani kingdom had split into five states.

 

• The Sultan acted on the forged letter produced by Gawan's enemies, and the old minister, then about seventy years old, was put to death, which created a lasting loss for the kingdom.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Gawan had conquered Konkan and Goa for the Bahmanis.

 

• The last Bahmani sultan, Kalimullah, fell about 1527.

 

• Muhammad Shah III's reign ran from about 1463 to 1482.

 

• Muhammad Shah III was only a young boy when he came to the throne, and Gawan acted as his guardian.

 

• The Bahmani kingdom declined very rapidly after 1481.

 

NOTE

 

• Firoz Shah Bahmani (Option 2): Firoz Shah ruled from 1397 to 1422, more than half a century before Gawan's death, so he cannot have ordered the execution.

 

• Ahmad Shah Wali (Option 3): Ahmad Shah Wali, who ruled in the 1420s-30s and shifted the capital to Bidar, died decades before Mahmud Gawan became minister, let alone before his execution.

 

• Mohammad Shah I (Option 4): Mohammad Shah I was the second Bahmani ruler in the fourteenth century and fought Bukka I; he belongs to the early phase of the kingdom, a century before Gawan's time.

question: Which Mughal emperor annexed the remaining Deccan kingdoms of Bijapur and Golconda during his Deccan campaign?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Aurangzeb.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Aurangzeb, during his long Deccan campaign, annexed the remaining successor states, with Bijapur falling in 1686 and Golconda in 1687 (औरंगज़ेब द्वारा बीजापुर और गोलकुंडा का विलय)

 

• These were two of the five states that had emerged from the Bahmani kingdom.

 

• His campaign ended the independent existence of the Deccan sultanates.

 

• Ahmadnagar had been reduced earlier, in Shah Jahan's reign.

 

• The fall of the two sultanates ended nearly two centuries of Deccan sultanate rule, but the long war drained Mughal resources and weakened the empire in the early eighteenth century.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Aurangzeb remained in the Deccan from 1681 until his death in 1707.

 

• Berar had been absorbed by Ahmadnagar in the sixteenth century, and Bidar by Bijapur in the seventeenth.

 

• The Qutb Shahi sultan Abul Hasan was the last ruler of Golconda.

 

• Aurangzeb's Deccan campaign began in 1681 and he died at Ahmadnagar in 1707.

 

• Abul Hasan Tana Shah was the last Qutb Shahi king.

 

NOTE

 

• Akbar (Option 1): Akbar began the Mughal advance in the Deccan, annexing Khandesh and part of Ahmadnagar, but Bijapur and Golconda remained independent in his reign.

 

• Jahangir (Option 2): Jahangir fought Malik Ambar of Ahmadnagar with limited success and did not annex either Bijapur or Golconda during his rule.

 

• Shah Jahan (Option 4): Shah Jahan crushed Ahmadnagar and forced Bijapur and Golconda to accept Mughal suzerainty, but their final annexation came later under his son Aurangzeb.

question: The chief cause of the long-drawn conflict between Vijayanagar and the Bahmani kingdom was the rivalry for:
option_4: The Raichur Doab between the Krishna and Tungabhadra
solution_text:
The correct answer is The Raichur Doab between the Krishna and Tungabhadra.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The long struggle centred on the fertile Raichur Doab, the land between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers (रायचूर दोआब — कृष्णा और तुंगभद्रा के बीच की उपजाऊ भूमि)

 

• Both the Bahmani sultans and the Vijayanagar kings coveted its rich agricultural produce and forts like Raichur and Mudgal.

 

• The doab lay on the frontier of the two states, so the dispute led to repeated wars and treaties.

 

• Krishnadevaraya's victory over the Bijapur ruler at Raichur in 1520 was one episode of this rivalry.

 

• The doab's rich black-soil farmland and its forts at Raichur and Mudgal gave the holder a strong strategic and economic base, so neither side was willing to give it up for long.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mohammad Shah I fought Bukka I; Firoz Shah fought Deva Raya I.

 

• Doab means the land between two rivers.

 

• The same area was disputed by later Deccan sultanates and Vijayanagar.

 

• The Krishna rises in the Western Ghats and flows east to the Bay of Bengal.

 

• The Tungabhadra is its major tributary in the south.

 

NOTE

 

• The Malabar pepper ports (Option 1): The Malabar pepper ports were on the west coast and mostly outside the Bahmani-Vijayanagar frontier; trade mattered, but the repeated wars were not fought for them.

 

• The Coromandel textile coast (Option 2): The Coromandel coast was a textile-trading region in the south-east, far from the Bahmani frontier zone, so it cannot explain the rivalry between these two neighbours.

 

• The salt pans of Gujarat (Option 3): Gujarat's salt pans lay in a distant western region under the Gujarat Sultanate and had nothing to do with the Deccan boundary dispute between the two states.

question: In the Battle of Raichur (1520), Krishnadevaraya of Vijayanagar defeated the ruler of:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bijapur.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• At Raichur in 1520, Krishnadevaraya defeated the Adil Shah of Bijapur (रायचूर का युद्ध 1520 — कृष्णदेव राय की बीजापुर पर विजय)

 

• The fighting arose out of the old struggle for the Raichur Doab between the Krishna and Tungabhadra.

 

• The victory made the Vijayanagar king the strongest power in the south in the sixteenth century.

 

• At this time the Bahmani kingdom itself had already broken up into five successor sultanates.

 

• After Raichur, Krishnadevaraya pushed further into the Bijapur country and took Gulbarga and Bidar, according to the standard accounts, which demonstrated the weakness of the divided Deccan sultanates.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Bijapur was ruled by the Adil Shahi dynasty founded by Yusuf Adil Shah.

 

• The reign of Krishnadevaraya lasted from 1509 to 1529.

 

• He was a contemporary of Babur, the first Mughal emperor.

 

• Ismail Adil Shah was the Bijapur ruler at the time.

 

• Raichur Fort changed hands many times between the Bahmanis and Vijayanagar.

 

NOTE

 

• Gujarat (Option 1): The Sultanate of Gujarat lay on the western coast and had no stake in the Raichur frontier; Vijayanagar's wars in this period were fought against the neighbouring Deccan states.

 

• Malwa (Option 3): Malwa was a central Indian sultanate far to the north; it was not involved in the struggle for the Raichur Doab with Vijayanagar during Krishnadevaraya's reign.

 

• Delhi (Option 4): Delhi was then under the Lodis and was not involved in the Deccan frontier contest; Krishnadevaraya's northern rival here was the Adil Shah of Bijapur.

question: The Vijayanagar regent Rama Raya was captured and executed in which battle of 1565?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Talikota.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Rama Raya was imprisoned and executed after the Battle of Talikota (1565), in which the combined Deccan Sultanates defeated Vijayanagar (तालीकोट का युद्ध 1565 — रामराय की पराजय)

 

• The city of Vijayanagar was destroyed and plundered, and the battle is generally taken to mark the end of the empire.

 

• The Sultanates in the alliance were Ahmadnagar, Bijapur, Golconda and Bidar.

 

• The kingdom, however, carried on under the Aravidu dynasty for about another century.

 

• The decisive defeat came even though Rama Raya, then very old, had a larger army; the standard accounts say that his Muslim contingents changed sides in mid-battle, and he was captured.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Talikota is also called Rakshasa-Tangadi in some accounts.

 

• Tirumala shifted the capital to Penukonda after the battle.

 

• The last ruler of Vijayanagar was Sriranga III.

 

• Rama Raya, also called Aliya Rama Raya, was son-in-law of Krishnadevaraya.

 

• Sadasiva Raya was the titular ruler at the time.

 

• Talikota is a small place in the Bijapur district of Karnataka, and the sultans' armies assembled near the Krishna.

 

NOTE

 

• Panipat (Option 1): Panipat saw battles in the north in 1526 (Babur vs Ibrahim Lodi), 1556 and 1761; none involved Vijayanagar or Rama Raya.

 

• Khanwa (Option 2): Khanwa (1527) was fought between Babur and Rana Sanga in Rajasthan; it belongs to the north Indian story and had no connection with the Vijayanagar regent.

 

• Chausa (Option 4): Chausa (1539) was a battle between Sher Shah Suri and Humayun in Bihar, nothing to do with Vijayanagar or the Deccan Sultanates.

question: Which traveller from Persia visited the court of Vijayanagar during the reign of Deva Raya II?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Abdur Razzak.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Abdur Razzak, the Persian envoy of the Timurid ruler Shah Rukh, visited Vijayanagar in the reign of Deva Raya II (अब्दुर रज़्ज़ाक — देवराय द्वितीय के समय पर्सियन यात्री)

 

• His account describes the grand city, the royal court and the empire's wealth.

 

• He is listed as Arab (Persian) in the notes' table of foreign travellers.

 

• The notes list Nicolo Conti, Paes and Barbosa under other rulers.

 

• His account of Vijayanagar mentions the seven concentric fortification walls, the market streets, and the great size and wealth of the capital that he saw at the Sangama court.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Abdur Razzak arrived in about 1443.

 

• Deva Raya II is regarded as the greatest Sangama ruler.

 

• Persian was the language of the Timurid court that sent him.

 

• Shah Rukh was the Timurid ruler of Herat and the son of Timur.

 

• Abdur Razzak's work is called Matla-us-Sadain.

 

• His narrative also notes the royal Mahanavami festival and the wealth of the capital's bazaars.

 

NOTE

 

• Nicolo Conti (Option 1): Nicolo Conti was a Venetian who visited during the reign of Deva Raya I, earlier than Deva Raya II; his nationality and ruler both differ from the question.

 

• Domingo Paes (Option 3): Domingo Paes was a Portuguese traveller associated with Krishnadevaraya in the early sixteenth century, not a Persian envoy of the fifteenth-century Sangama king.

 

• Barbosa (Option 4): Barbosa was also Portuguese and is linked with Krishnadevaraya; he came to the west coast and described Vijayanagar from there, not as a Persian visitor of Deva Raya II.

question: Which Vijayanagar king was visited by the Portuguese traveller Domingo Paes?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Krishnadevaraya.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Domingo Paes, a Portuguese traveller, visited Vijayanagar during the reign of Krishnadevaraya and left a detailed description of the capital (डोमिंगो पेस — कृष्णदेव राय के काल का पुर्तगाली यात्री)

 

• The notes list both Paes and Barbosa against Krishnadevaraya.

 

• Their accounts reflect the contact between Vijayanagar and the Portuguese on the west coast.

 

• Krishnadevaraya reigned from 1509 to 1529.

 

• Paes described the capital as one of the best-provided cities in the world and left an account of its markets, festival of Mahanavami, and the king's palaces and army.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Fernao Nuniz, another Portuguese, later wrote a chronicle of Vijayanagar.

 

• Duarte Barbosa was a Portuguese writer on the Indian coast.

 

• Albuquerque was the Portuguese governor of the time.

 

• Paes and Nuniz's accounts were later brought together in Robert Sewell's A Forgotten Empire.

 

• Duarte Barbosa travelled along the west coast of India around 1500-1516.

 

NOTE

 

• Deva Raya I (Option 1): Deva Raya I was visited by the Venetian Nicolo Conti in the early fifteenth century, a century before the Portuguese travellers arrived in India.

 

• Deva Raya II (Option 2): Deva Raya II received the Persian envoy Abdur Razzak, and he ruled in the mid-fifteenth century, before the Portuguese had reached India by sea.

 

• Harihara I (Option 4): Harihara I was the founder in 1336 and is linked in the notes with the Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta, not with Portuguese visitors of the sixteenth century.

question: The Kamalapuram Tank, an example of Vijayanagar water management, was built by:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Krishnadevaraya.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Kamalapuram tank was built by Krishnadevaraya; Vijayanagar was famous for its stepped tanks and irrigation works (कमलापुरम टैंक — कृष्णदेव राय द्वारा निर्मित)

 

• He is credited with building tanks and canals on the Tungabhadra, which increased farm output.

 

• The tank shows the empire's concern with water supply for the capital and for cultivation.

 

• The same king raised the Vitthala and Hazara Rama temples at Hampi.

 

• The notes tie the king's building programme to useful public works, and this tank is among the best known of his hydraulic works that supplied water to the capital.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The stepped tank at Hampi near the royal centre is a famous structure.

 

• Nagalapuram is another town he founded.

 

• Krishnadevaraya ruled for twenty years, from 1509 to 1529.

 

• Kamalapuram lies close to Hampi in Ballari district.

 

• Vijayanagar engineers built dams and canals from the Tungabhadra to bring water to the royal centre.

 

NOTE

 

• Deva Raya II (Option 1): Deva Raya II is celebrated for military reforms and the visit of Abdur Razzak, but the Kamalapuram tank is attributed in the notes to Krishnadevaraya, a Tuluva king.

 

• Saluva Narasimha (Option 2): Saluva Narasimha founded a short-lived dynasty that is remembered for seizing power; irrigation works like the Kamalapuram tank are not credited to him.

 

• Rama Raya (Option 3): Rama Raya was the Aravidu regent who died at Talikota in 1565 and is remembered for politics and war, not for the tank near Hampi.
